Empirical Research Plan: “The Impact of NAFTA on U.S. Local Labor-Market Wages and Employment”

================================================================
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy – Difference-in-Differences (DID) with continuous treatment intensity.  
• “Time” dimension: before NAFTA (1990 Census reference week) vs. after NAFTA (2000 Census reference week).  
• “Cross-section” dimension: U.S. commuting zones (CZs) that differ in the ex-ante intensity with which their industries were hit by NAFTA tariff cuts.  

Why DID is appropriate  
1. NAFTA was enacted at a single, well-defined date (1994), creating a sharp break.  
2. Tariff reductions varied mechanically across industries according to the tariff schedules negotiated years earlier; local exposure therefore varies predictably with each CZ’s pre-1994 industry mix.  
3. We observe repeated cross-sections of individuals in identical geographic units both before and after the policy.  

Extension / robustness: Instrumental-variables (IV) “shift–share” design, where actual post-1994 Mexican import penetration is instrumented with the tariff-reduction-based exposure index. This addresses possible endogeneity of realized imports while preserving the DID timing.

================================================================
2. Treatment and Control Definition
----------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable (continuous)  
Expos_c  ≡  Σ_i ( EmpShare_i,c,1990  ×  TariffCut_i,US→MX )  
• EmpShare_i,c,1990 = share of CZ c’s employment in 1990 that is in industry i (4-digit SIC/NAICS harmonised).  
• TariffCut_i = percent-point fall in the statutory U.S. MFN tariff on imports from Mexico between 1993 and NAFTA phase-out completion (industry-specific).  
Higher Expos_c ⇒ larger predicted competitive shock from Mexico.  

Binary version for some tables: Treated = CZ in the top quartile (or above the median) of Expos_c; Control = CZ in the bottom quartile (or bottom half). Results are virtually identical when exploiting the continuous measure.

Treatment timing  
Post_t  = 1 for observations drawn from the 2000 Census; 0 for 1990 Census.

Regression cell = individual j in CZ c at time t.

================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends.  
In the absence of NAFTA, high- and low-exposure CZs would have experienced similar wage/employment trends.  
Plausibility: 1990 industrial composition predates NAFTA and cannot react to it. We will test parallelism using 1980-1990 data as a pre-period placebo.

A2. Exogeneity of tariff-cut schedule.  
Tariff reductions were negotiated at the national level and are orthogonal to subsequent local shocks. Plausible because they primarily reflect cross-industry political bargains, not CZ-specific conditions.

A3. No large spillovers across CZs (SUTVA).  
Workers in a low-exposure CZ are not substantially affected by shocks to neighboring high-exposure CZs. Possibly violated if displaced workers migrate. We check robustness by weighting individuals by their CZ’s 1990 population (i.e., a “fixed-population” view).

A4. Stable industry shares within CZ between 1990 and treatment.  
Because we lock in the 1990 shares, the treatment variable is predetermined. This satisfies the standard “Bartik” symmetry condition.

================================================================
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
----------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential pre-trends unrelated to NAFTA (e.g., technology, China shock).  
Mitigation:  
• Graph and formally test 1980-1990 trends; include industry-specific national time trends.  
• Add controls for China import penetration (Autor-Dorn-Hanson exposure) interacted with Post_t.  

T2. Selective migration or changes in CZ boundaries.  
Mitigation:  
• Use 1990 population weights (shift-share “long-differences” on a fixed cohort).  
• Show results for non-movers identified in the Census long-form questions on residence five years earlier.  

T3. Measurement error in tariff cuts or employment shares.  
Mitigation:  
• Use alternative tariff sources (USITC, Feenstra customs data).  
• Instrument realized imports with tariff cuts in IV robustness to attenuate measurement error bias.

================================================================
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(data.table)        # fast data handling
library(fixest)            # fixed-effects estimators
library(haven)             # if reading Stata dta files
library(modelsummary)      # for neat tables

# ---- 1. Load Census micro data ----
p90 <- fread("pums_1990.csv")   # include CZ identifier cz
p00 <- fread("pums_2000.csv")

# ---- 2. Load industry tariffs and construct exposure ----
tar <- fread("nafta_tariff_cuts.csv")     # vars: ind, tariff_cut
share <- fread("cz_ind_emp_share_1990.csv")  # vars: cz, ind, emp_share90

# merge and compute exposure by CZ
expo <- merge(share, tar, by = "ind")
expo[, expos := emp_share90 * tariff_cut ]
cz_expo <- expo[, .(exposure = sum(expos)), by = cz]

# ---- 3. Stack individual data sets ----
p90[, year := 1990]; p00[, year := 2000]
pums <- rbindlist(list(p90, p00), use.names = TRUE, fill = TRUE)

# add exposure to each individual
pums <- merge(pums, cz_expo, by = "cz")

# ---- 4. Variable construction ----
pums[, post := as.integer(year == 2000)]
pums[, l_wage := log(wage_inc)]                   # hourly or annual real wage
pums[, emp := as.integer(employed == 1)]          # 1=working, 0=not
# demographic controls
pums[, educ_fe := factor(educ)]
pums[, agegrp  := cut(age, c(18,25,35,45,55,65,100), right = FALSE)]

# ---- 5. Main DID regression ----
did_main <- feols(l_wage ~ post * exposure + age + I(age^2) + educ_fe + factor(sex) |
                  cz + factor(year),
                  data = pums, weights = ~perwt, cluster = ~cz)

etable(did_main, title = "Main DID: Wage Effects of NAFTA Exposure")

# Employment analogous:
did_emp <- feols(emp ~ post * exposure + age + I(age^2) + educ_fe + factor(sex) |
                 cz + factor(year),
                 data = pums, weights = ~perwt, cluster = ~cz)

# ---- 6. Event-study robustness using additional years (if 1980 available) ----
# here only skeleton
# es <- feols(l_wage ~ i(rel_year, exposure) + controls | cz + year, data = ...)

# ---- 7. IV robustness: Instrument import penetration with exposure ----
# suppose 'imp_pen' is Δ Mexican imports / domestic absorption at CZ level
cz_imp <- fread("cz_import_penetration_2000.csv")        # cz, imp_pen
cz_dat <- merge(cz_imp, cz_expo, by = "cz")
iv <- feols(l_wage ~ post * imp_pen | cz + year | post * exposure ~ post * imp_pen,
            data = merge(pums, cz_dat, by = "cz"), cluster = ~cz)

# ---- 8. Save results ----
modelsummary(list(did_main, did_emp, iv),
             output = "results/nafta_cz_effects.docx")
```

================================================================
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------------------
Theory (Heckscher-Ohlin/Stolper-Samuelson) predicts that U.S. low-skill intensive industries lose from trade liberalisation with Mexico, which has relatively abundant low-skill labour.  
Prediction:  
• Real wages of production-type workers in high-exposure CZs fall relative to low-exposure CZs (≈ 2–3 percent).  
• Employment/population ratio declines by roughly 3–5 percentage points in most-exposed CZs over the decade.  
Higher-skill workers may be unaffected or gain slightly; we will probe heterogeneity.

================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
----------------------------------------------------------------
C1. No differential pre-trends …………………… 0.8 (we can test and largely support)  
C2. Treatment exogenous to outcome shocks …… 0.9 (tariff schedule predetermined)  
C3. No spillovers / SUTVA ………………………… 0.5 (migration & input linkages possible)  
C4. Composition stable / no selective sorting … 0.7 (use fixed-pop weights, but not perfect)  
C5. Correct specification & robust SEs ………… 1.0 (cluster at CZ, multiple robustness)  

Total ≈ 3.9 / 5 – credible but not bullet-proof.

================================================================
This plan delivers a transparent and replicable approach to estimating the causal effect of NAFTA-induced tariff reductions on U.S. local wages and employment.
